findings.matters: A lender sees a critical service (waste collection) running at higher cost than the council anticipated, with the council resorting to agency staff. This signals either understaffed budgets, recruitment failure, or poor cost control.

findings.detail: The council has ceased a trading service entirely due to ongoing challenges and forthcoming government legislation. The service forecasted a £188,000 loss this year and was judged unsustainable, signalling both current losses and an expectation of structural pressure ahead.
findings.matters: Service closures matter to a lender because they often indicate that the council cannot compete or is unable to adapt a line of business to regulatory change. It also confirms a material revenue stream is gone.

findings.headline: Revenues and Benefits has lost government grant funding, creating a £463,000 structural overspend

findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether core service funding is stable. Loss of grant revenue that does not return is a structural deterioration in the council's financial position.

findings.paper_title: 06b Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Draft

findings.detail: Rather than external borrowing, the council has been using cash reserves to fund capital expenditure. This approach reduces available investment balances (from £11.3m to £15.4m over the recent period) and the income earned from those investments. The council proposes charging interest to internally-funded projects to offset this.

findings.matters: This substantial increase in debt obligations will materially increase the council's annual interest costs and changes its financial position, which affects both creditworthiness and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: External debt at 31 March 2026: £10,837k; expected change 2026/27: +£12,774k; projected 31 March 2027: £23,611k

This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will cost further £1m over 2026/27 and 2027/28; full scope unclear
findings.detail: The council previously set aside £209k revenue budget and £200k reserve for LGR transition. It now proposes a further £1m to be split across 2026/27 and 2027/28. The report notes that inflation has 'often been higher' than budget assumption in recent years and that service managers are expected to 'manage within their overall cash limit'.
findings.matters: This is a recipe for hidden overspends if managers cannot absorb the 0.95% annual gap. The council is essentially under-budgeting inflationary pressure and relying on services to absorb it.

findings.detail: The previous budget assumed Council Tax base would grow by 730 Band D equivalent properties annually, based on housing needs assessment. Actual growth in recent years has been only 97 properties. The budget has been revised to assume this lower rate for all three years ahead.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Treasury Management Mid Year Report v3
findings.headline: Capital programme is under active review and subject to revision due to inflationary pressure and supply-chain constraints, creating uncertainty in final borrowing need.
findings.detail: The council states that its £29.779m capital programme 'is being kept under review due to the effects of inflationary pressure, shortages of materials and labour'. The council signals that its 'borrowing strategy will, therefore, also be regularly reviewed and revised, if necessary, to achieve the progression of the Capital Programme.' This indicates the current revised budget and borrowing forecasts may not be final, and the council may revise both downward if projects cannot proceed, or upward if inflation pushes costs higher.
findings.matters: A capital programme and borrowing forecast that is actively under review creates uncertainty for lenders evaluating the council's medium-term debt trajectory. Execution risk on £29.779m of capital spending means the £20.421m borrowing forecast is contingent on programme delivery that the council itself does not yet regard as certain.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Treasury Management Mid Year Report v3
findings.headline: Council is deferring borrowing despite a £72.615m underlying capital financing requirement and plans to enter the market later in the year.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying need to borrow for capital) stands at £72.615m, up from £59.006m originally. However, actual external borrowings remain just £14.514m. The council states it is using cash flow in lieu of borrowing as 'prudent and cost-effective in the current economic climate' but notes this 'will require ongoing monitoring if gilt yields remain elevated'. The council explicitly states 'It is anticipated that further borrowing may be undertaken during this financial year subject to the progression of the Capital Programme.'
findings.matters: The council is timing a £57m+ borrowing entry into the market later in the year, creating concentration and timing risk. If gilt yields remain elevated or deteriorate, the council could face significantly higher interest costs than it would have incurred by borrowing earlier at lower rates, or face market access issues if conditions tighten.

findings.paper_title: 07 - Treasury Management Mid Year Report v3

To finance this £9.4m increase, the council expected to draw on capital receipts, but actual receipts collapsed from £10.118m to £2.300m. Combined with a £9.4m spending increase, the shortfall in receipts forced the borrowing requirement from £8.286m to £20.421m.
findings.matters: A 44% capital spending increase coupled with a significant shortfall in capital receipts (a 77% drop from forecast) signals that the council's asset disposal strategy or capital receipts generation is underperforming. The council must now borrow substantially to fund plans it expected to self-finance, materially changing its debt trajectory.

news_drafts.headline: Sevenoaks budget paper says no expectation that a Section 114 notice will be needed
news_drafts.lead:
Sevenoaks District Council's transition budget report says there is "currently no expectation that the Council would be required to be in that position", referring to the issuing of a Section 114 notice. The report went to the Finance & Investment Advisory Committee on 10 November 2026.

The statement is in the report's legal implications section. That section says that failure to set a balanced budget could lead to a Section 114 notice, the formal notice a council's chief finance officer issues when the council cannot balance its budget. The notice would be issued by the council's Section 151 Officer, its chief finance officer.

The report lists the risks as uncertainty about the size of the shortfall and uncertainty about the timing of the financial settlement. It gives no figure for the shortfall in the material reviewed.

news_drafts.headline: Sevenoaks projects £250k deficit as service costs rise and reserves drain
news_drafts.lead: Sevenoaks Council is forecasting a £250,000 deficit for the year to March 2027, a material shift from its break-even budget after four months of the financial year. Service spending has overrun by £244,000, with particular pressure in planning and regulatory services, partly offset by strong investment returns of £165,000. The council's usable reserves, money set aside for planned spending, have been drawn down by £841,000 in the first four months alone, with the Financial Plan Reserve depleted by 18 per cent. At the current rate, total reserves would fall by approximately £2.5 million over a full year. The deficit includes the impact of a 3.3 per cent pay award still under negotiation, estimated to cost £71,000 beyond budget. The council's treasury management, including investments in multi-asset income funds and a housing loan portfolio, is performing well but cannot fully offset the underlying operational pressures.
